claim: Nuclear factor 90 (NF90) is a novel virus sensor that serves to initiate antiviral innate immunity by triggering stress granule (SG) formation.
source: Nuclear factor 90 (NF90) is a novel virus sensor that serves to initiate antiviral innate immunity by triggering stress granule (SG) formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing NF90's role as a virus sensor and SG trigger.

claim: Tim-3 promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of NF90.
source: We found that Tim-3, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of NF90 and inhibits NF90-SG-mediated antiviral immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing Tim-3-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of NF90.

claim: Tim-3 inhibits NF90-SG-mediated antiviral immunity.
source: We found that Tim-3, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, promotes the ubiquitination and degradation of NF90 and inhibits NF90-SG-mediated antiviral immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased viral loads and enhanced SG formation in Tim-3 knockout cells.

claim: Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) infection induces the up-regulation and activation of Tim-3 in macrophages.
source: Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) infection induces the up-regulation and activation of Tim-3 in macrophages, which in turn recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM47 to the zinc finger domain of NF90 and initiate a proteasome-dependent degradation via K48-linked ubiquitination at Lys297.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B, and C demonstrating increased Tim-3 expression and phosphorylation after VSV infection.

claim: Tim-3 recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM47 to the zinc finger domain of NF90.
source: Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) infection induces the up-regulation and activation of Tim-3 in macrophages, which in turn recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM47 to the zinc finger domain of NF90 and initiate a proteasome-dependent degradation via K48-linked ubiquitination at Lys297.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing interactions between Tim-3, TRIM47, and the DZF domain of NF90.

claim: Tim-3 initiates proteasome-dependent degradation of NF90 via K48-linked ubiquitination at Lys297.
source: Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) infection induces the up-regulation and activation of Tim-3 in macrophages, which in turn recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM47 to the zinc finger domain of NF90 and initiate a proteasome-dependent degradation via K48-linked ubiquitination at Lys297.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assays and site-directed mutagenesis experiments showing K48-linked ubiquitination at Lys297.

claim: Targeted inactivation of Tim-3 enhances NF90 downstream SG formation by selectively increasing the phosphorylation of protein kinase R and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α.
source: Targeted inactivation of Tim-3 enhances the NF90 downstream SG formation by selectively increasing the phosphorylation of protein kinase R and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α, the expression of SG markers G3BP1 and TIA-1, and protecting mice from VSV challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6A showing increased phosphorylation of PKR and eIF2α in Tim-3KO cells.

claim: Targeted inactivation of Tim-3 increases the expression of SG markers G3BP1 and TIA-1.
source: Targeted inactivation of Tim-3 enhances the NF90 downstream SG formation by selectively increasing the phosphorylation of protein kinase R and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α, the expression of SG markers G3BP1 and TIA-1, and protecting mice from VSV challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B and C showing increased G3BP1 and TIA-1 expression in Tim-3KO cells.

claim: Targeted inactivation of Tim-3 protects mice from VSV challenge.
source: Targeted inactivation of Tim-3 enhances the NF90 downstream SG formation by selectively increasing the phosphorylation of protein kinase R and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α, the expression of SG markers G3BP1 and TIA-1, and protecting mice from VSV challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data in Figure 7J showing increased survival of Tim-3KO mice after VSV infection.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), are main sensors in defending virus infection.
source: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), are main sensors in defending virus infection (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: PRR-mediated downstream signaling pathways initiating an anti-viral innate immune response is the classic anti-virus infection model.
source: PRR-mediated downstream signaling pathways initiating an anti-viral innate immune response is the classic anti-virus infection model (Barbalat et al., 2011; McFadden et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barbalat et al., 2011 and McFadden et al., 2017.

claim: NF90 is encoded by interleukin enhancer-binding factor-3.
source: Recently, studies have found that nuclear factor 90 (NF90), which is encoded by interleukin enhancer-binding factor-3, is a critical sensor for invading viruses (Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009; Wen et al., 2014; Pfeifer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: NF90 is a critical sensor for invading viruses.
source: Recently, studies have found that nuclear factor 90 (NF90), which is encoded by interleukin enhancer-binding factor-3, is a critical sensor for invading viruses (Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009; Wen et al., 2014; Pfeifer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009; Wen et al., 2014; Pfeifer et al., 2008.

claim: NF90 is an evolutionarily conserved member of the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)-binding protein family.
source: NF90 is an evolutionarily conserved member of the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)-binding protein family and is abundantly expressed in various mammalian cells (Patiño et al., 2015; Masuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Patiño et al., 2015 and Masuda et al., 2013.

claim: NF90 is abundantly expressed in various mammalian cells.
source: NF90 is an evolutionarily conserved member of the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)-binding protein family and is abundantly expressed in various mammalian cells (Patiño et al., 2015; Masuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Patiño et al., 2015 and Masuda et al., 2013.

claim: NF90 recognizes virus dsRNA and triggers the formation of stress granules (SGs).
source: As an important antiviral pathway, NF90 recognizes virus dsRNA and triggers the formation of stress granules (SGs), which are composed of cytoplasmic particles including ribonucleoproteins, RNA-binding proteins, and translation initiation factors (Shi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2007.

claim: Stress granules are composed of cytoplasmic particles including ribonucleoproteins, RNA-binding proteins, and translation initiation factors.
source: As an important antiviral pathway, NF90 recognizes virus dsRNA and triggers the formation of stress granules (SGs), which are composed of cytoplasmic particles including ribonucleoproteins, RNA-binding proteins, and translation initiation factors (Shi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2007.

claim: A growing number of virus families modulate SG formation and function to maximize replication efficiency.
source: Unfortunately, a growing number of virus families modulate SG formation and function to maximize replication efficiency (White and Lloyd, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to White and Lloyd, 2012.

claim: Upon sensing virus, NF90 induces the phosphorylation of dsRNA-activated protein kinase R (PKR).
source: Upon sensing virus, NF90 induces the phosphorylation of dsRNA-activated protein kinase R (PKR) (Li et al., 2016; Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016 and Wen et al., 2014.

claim: SGs form following PKR-mediated phosphorylation and activation of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α (eIF2α).
source: Then SGs form following PKR-mediated phosphorylation and activation of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α (eIF2α), which induces the expression of G3BP1 (Tsai et al., 2017) (Ras-GAP SH3-binding protein-1) and TIA-1 (T-cell intracellular antigen-1), two key markers in SGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2017.

claim: Phosphorylation and activation of eIF2α induces the expression of G3BP1 and TIA-1, two key markers in SGs.
source: Then SGs form following PKR-mediated phosphorylation and activation of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α (eIF2α), which induces the expression of G3BP1 (Tsai et al., 2017) (Ras-GAP SH3-binding protein-1) and TIA-1 (T-cell intracellular antigen-1), two key markers in SGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2017.

claim: The activated eIF2α co-operates with other components of SGs to block virus mRNA translation.
source: The activated eIF2α co-operates with other components of SGs to block virus mRNA translation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of SG function.

claim: Tim-3 is encoded by the hepatitis A virus cellular receptor two gene (Havcr2).
source: Tim-3, encoded by the hepatitis A virus cellular receptor two gene (Havcr2), is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that was first identified in activated T cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tim-3.

claim: Tim-3 is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that was first identified in activated T cells.
source: Tim-3, encoded by the hepatitis A virus cellular receptor two gene (Havcr2), is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that was first identified in activated T cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Tim-3.

claim: Tim-3 is expressed in innate immune cells, such as dendritic cells and macrophages.
source: Later, Tim-3 was also found to be expressed in innate immune cells, such as dendritic cells and macrophages (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2013.

claim: Tim-3 is an exhaustion marker in immune cells of both tumors and infectious diseases.
source: Establishment of Tim-3 as an exhaustion marker in immune cells of both tumors and infectious diseases makes Tim-3 an attractive target for immunotherapy similar to PD-1 (Huang et al., 2015), CTLA-4 (Stamper et al., 2001), and Siglec-G (Rangachari et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2015; Stamper et al., 2001; and Rangachari et al., 2012.

claim: Increased Tim-3 expression on immune cells in patients with coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is associated with an exhaustion phenotype.
source: Recently, a report showed that increased Tim-3 expression on immune cells in patients with coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is associated with an exhaustion phenotype (Diao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diao et al., 2020.

claim: Tim-3 does not have an inhibitory motif within its tail.
source: However, Tim-3 does not have an inhibitory motif within its tail (van de Weyer et al., 2006), and the mechanism by which Tim-3 mediates inhibitory signaling remains largely unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van de Weyer et al., 2006.

claim: CEACAM1 is a heterophilic ligand of Tim-3 and is required for Tim-3 to mediate T cell inhibition.
source: Huang et al., 2015 showed that CEACAM1 is a heterophilic ligand of Tim-3 and is required for Tim-3 to mediate T cell inhibition and that Bat-3 acts as a safety catch, which blocks Tim-3-mediated inhibitory signals in T cells (Rangachari et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2015 and Rangachari et al., 2012.

claim: Bat-3 acts as a safety catch, which blocks Tim-3-mediated inhibitory signals in T cells.
source: Huang et al., 2015 showed that CEACAM1 is a heterophilic ligand of Tim-3 and is required for Tim-3 to mediate T cell inhibition and that Bat-3 acts as a safety catch, which blocks Tim-3-mediated inhibitory signals in T cells (Rangachari et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2015 and Rangachari et al., 2012.

claim: Ubiquitination is one of the most versatile posttranslational modifications and is indispensable for antiviral infection.
source: Ubiquitination is one of the most versatile posttranslational modifications and is indispensable for antiviral infection (Heaton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heaton et al., 2016.

claim: Ubiquitination plays important roles in various cellular processes, including cell proliferation and antiviral innate signaling.
source: Increasing evidences suggest that ubiquitination plays important roles in various cellular processes, including cell proliferation and antiviral innate signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ubiquitination.

claim: Posttranslational modification of TRAF3/6, RIG-I, MAVS, TBK1, IRF3/7, and NLRP3 by different types of ubiquitination plays key roles in the regulation of antiviral innate immunity.
source: Posttranslational modification of many signaling molecules, including TRAF3/6 (Chen et al., 2015), RIG-I (Chen et al., 2013), MAVS (Liu et al., 2017), TBK1 (Song et al., 2016a), IRF3/7 (Yu and Hayward, 2010; Wang et al., 2015), and NLRP3 (Song et al., 2016b), involved in TLR, RLR, and NLR pathways by different types of ubiquitination plays key roles in the regulation of antiviral innate immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2017; Song et al., 2016a; Yu and Hayward, 2010; Wang et al., 2015; and Song et al., 2016b.

claim: NF90 contains a ubiquitin-binding domain (domain associated with zinc fingers, DZF).
source: However, whether NF90, a molecule containing a ubiquitin-binding domain (domain associated with zinc fingers, DZF), undergoes ubiquitination remains unclear.
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of NF90.

claim: Tim-3 was involved in innate immunity against vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) by promoting the proteasomal degradation of NF90 via the tripartite motif-containing protein 47 (TRIM47)-mediated conjugation of K48-linked ubiquitin.
source: Here we found that Tim-3 was involved in innate immunity against vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) by promoting the proteasomal degradation of NF90 via the tripartite motif-containing protein 47 (TRIM47)-mediated conjugation of K48-linked ubiquitin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: This is the first time demonstrating ubiquitination as a new posttranslational modification mechanism of NF90.
source: To the best of our knowledge, it is the first time demonstrating ubiquitination as a new posttranslational modification mechanism of NF90.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: VSV infection induces the up-regulation of Tim-3 in macrophages.
source: Shortly after VSV challenge, the expression of Tim-3 was upregulated in macrophages (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: VSV infection induces time-dependent enhancement of Tim-3 phosphorylation in HEK293T cells transfected with Tim-3.
source: There was a time-dependent enhancement of Tim-3 phosphorylation in HEK293T cells transfected with Tim-3 and challenged with VSV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Knockout of Tim-3 in macrophages leads to decreased VSV load.
source: Both knockout and knockdown of Tim-3 in macrophages led to a decreased VSV load (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 assay data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Knockdown of Tim-3 in macrophages leads to decreased VSV load.
source: Both knockout and knockdown of Tim-3 in macrophages led to a decreased VSV load (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCID50 assay data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Tim-3 has a negative regulatory role in anti-viral innate immunity.
source: These findings suggest a negative regulatory role of Tim-3 in anti-viral innate immunity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing decreased viral loads in Tim-3 knockout/knockdown cells.

claim: NF90 received the highest score and the highest number of matched peptides among Tim-3-interacting protein candidates identified by mass spectrometry.
source: Among the candidates, NF90, an RNA-binding protein involved in anti-infection and anti-tumor immunity, received the highest score and the highest number of matched peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tim-3 interacts with NF90.
source: To confirm the interaction between Tim-3 and NF90, HEK293T cells were co-transfected with NF90 and Tim-3 and immunoprecipitation was conducted targeting either Tim-3 (Figure 2A) or NF90 (Figure 2B); all confirmed the interaction between Tim-3 and NF90.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: 4Y/F mutants of Tim-3 (Y265F, Y272F, Y280F, Y281F) weaken the binding of Tim-3 with NF90.
source: The results showed that 4Y/F mutants of Tim-3 (Y265F, Y272F, Y280F, Y281F) weakened the binding of Tim-3 with NF90, while deletion of the intracellular domain of Tim-3 (△IC) resulted in the loss of binding activity of Tim-3 with NF90 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Deletion of the intracellular domain of Tim-3 (△IC) results in the loss of binding activity of Tim-3 with NF90.
source: The results showed that 4Y/F mutants of Tim-3 (Y265F, Y272F, Y280F, Y281F) weakened the binding of Tim-3 with NF90, while deletion of the intracellular domain of Tim-3 (△IC) resulted in the loss of binding activity of Tim-3 with NF90 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Tim-3 interacts with NF90 through its intracellular domain, in which Y265, Y272, Y280, and Y281 play an important role.
source: These data showed that Tim-3 interacts with NF90 through its intracellular domain, in which Y265, Y272, Y280, and Y281 play an important role.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing weakened binding with Y/F mutants.

claim: Overexpression of Tim-3 decreases the expression of NF90.
source: In HEK293T cells transfected with Tim-3 or in macrophages from Tim-3 transgenic (Tim-3-TG) mice, the overexpression of Tim-3 decreased the expression of NF90 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The total ubiquitination of NF90 is significantly increased in macrophages from Tim-3-TG mice compared to those from WT mice.
source: Interestingly, the total ubiquitination and the k48-linked ubiquitination of NF90 were significantly increased in macrophages from Tim-3-TG mice compared to those from WT mice (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The K48-linked ubiquitination of NF90 is significantly increased in macrophages from Tim-3-TG mice compared to those from WT mice.
source: Interestingly, the total ubiquitination and the k48-linked ubiquitination of NF90 were significantly increased in macrophages from Tim-3-TG mice compared to those from WT mice (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: NF90 undergoes K48-linked ubiquitination, which can be enhanced by co-transfected Tim-3.
source: When NF90, K48-Ub, or Tim-3 was transfected into HEK293T cells, NF90 underwent K48-linked ubiquitination, which can be enhanced by co-transfected Tim-3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The DZF domain of NF90 is dominantly ubiquitinated.
source: We then explored the domain of NF90 for ubiquitination using constructions encoding the DZF domain, full-length NF90 or NF90 lacking the DZF domain (△DZF) (Figure 3C) and found that the DZF domain of NF90 was dominantly ubiquitinated (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tim-3 specially enhances the ubiquitination of the DZF domain of NF90.
source: Finally, when the plasmid of Tim-3 was co-transfected with different NF90 constructs, the data revealed that Tim-3 specially enhanced the ubiquitination of DZF (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NF90 can be ubiquitinated at the DZF domain, and the process can be enhanced by Tim-3.
source: These results demonstrated that NF90 can be ubiquitinated at the DZF domain, and the process can be enhanced by Tim-3, suggesting that Tim-3 may suppress NF90 by promoting its ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing enhanced ubiquitination of the DZF domain in the presence of Tim-3.

claim: TRIM47 had the highest Mascot scores and the highest number of matched peptides among NF90-interacting protein candidates with potential E3 ligase activities.
source: Among the NF90-interacting protein candidates, we identified three proteins with potential E3 ligase activities. TRIM47 had the highest Mascot scores and the highest number of matched peptides (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knockdown of TRIM47 with specific siRNA in macrophages increases the half-life of endogenous NF90 protein during VSV infection.
source: Knockdown of TRIM47 with specific small interfering RNA(siRNA) (si-TRIM47) in macrophages increased the half-life of endogenous NF90 protein during VSV infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRIM47 induces degradation of NF90 in a dose-dependent manner, which can be blockaded in the presence of MG132.
source: TRIM47 induced degradation of NF90 in a dose-dependent manner, which can be blockaded in the presence of MG132, indicating a proteasome-dependent degradation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tim-3 dose-dependently enhances TRIM47-mediated degradation of NF90.
source: In addition, when Tim-3 was co-transfected, it dose-dependently enhanced TRIM47-mediated degradation of NF90 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: VSV challenge leads to decreased TRIM47 expression in Tim-3KO cells compared with that in WT cells.
source: VSV challenge led to decreased TRIM47 expression in Tim-3KO cells compared with that in WT cells (Figure 4D) and increased TRIM47 expression in Tim-3 transgenic mice-derived macrophages compared with that in control cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: VSV challenge leads to increased TRIM47 expression in Tim-3 transgenic mice-derived macrophages compared with that in control cells.
source: VSV challenge led to decreased TRIM47 expression in Tim-3KO cells compared with that in WT cells (Figure 4D) and increased TRIM47 expression in Tim-3 transgenic mice-derived macrophages compared with that in control cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tim-3 promotes the expression of TRIM47 in the presence of virus.
source: These results showed that Tim-3 promotes the expression of TRIM47 in the presence of virus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing differential TRIM47 expression in Tim-3KO and Tim-3-TG cells after VSV infection.

claim: TRIM47 undergoes ubiquitination when Tim-3 is overexpressed.
source: Interestingly, when the genes encoding TRIM47, Tim-3, and Ub-K63 were co-transfected into HEK293T cells, TRIM47 underwent ubiquitination, and Tim-3 enhanced this progress (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Tim-3 enhances the ubiquitination of TRIM47.
source: Interestingly, when the genes encoding TRIM47, Tim-3, and Ub-K63 were co-transfected into HEK293T cells, TRIM47 underwent ubiquitination, and Tim-3 enhanced this progress (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: TRIM47 interacts with the intracellular domain of Tim-3.
source: The immunoprecipitation assay showed that TRIM47 interacts with the intracellular domain of Tim-3 and with the DZF domain of NF90.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TRIM47 interacts with the DZF domain of NF90.
source: The immunoprecipitation assay showed that TRIM47 interacts with the intracellular domain of Tim-3 and with the DZF domain of NF90.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tim-3 recruits TRIM47 to the DZF domain via its intracellular domain while forming a complex of TRIM47 and NF90.
source: These data suggest that Tim-3 recruits TRIM47 to the DZF domain via its intracellular domain while forming a complex of TRIM47 and NF90.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the interaction data showing Tim-3 binds to both TRIM47 and NF90.

claim: Overexpression of TRIM47 promotes the ubiquitination of NF90, and this process is enhanced when Tim-3 is co-transfected.
source: Overexpression of TRIM47 promotes the ubiquitination of NF90, and this process was enhanced when Tim-3 was co-transfected (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: K297 is the critical residue for the ubiquitination of NF90-DZF targeted by TRIM47.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that K297 is the critical residue for the ubiquitination of NF90-DZF targeted by TRIM47.
evidence: This claim is supported by site-directed mutagenesis data showing that K297R mutation blocks ubiquitination.

claim: Only mutations of arginine at K297R completely blocked the TRIM47-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of NF90 via a K48-mediated linkage.
source: We further demonstrated that only mutations of arginine at K297R completely blocked the TRIM47-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of NF90 via a K48-mediated linkage (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TRIM47 dose-dependently induces the degradation of NF90 DZF domain but not of DZF K297R.
source: In addition, when co-transfected K48-Ub, Tim-3, wild-type NF90, DZF domain, or DZF K297R with increased doses of TRIM47, we found that TRIM47 dose-dependently induced the degradation of NF90 DZF domain but not of DZF K297R (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The expression of NF90 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α and PKR are dramatically increased in macrophages from Tim-3KO mice compared with those in cells from WT mice.
source: The data in Figure 6A show that the expression of NF90 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α and PKR were dramatically increased in macrophages from Tim-3KO mice compared with those in cells from WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is no difference in p38 and ERK phosphorylation between Tim-3KO and WT cells.
source: There was no difference in p38 and ERK phosphorylation between Tim-3KO and WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tim-3 knockout significantly increases the expression of G3BP1 and TIA-1 at the protein level in macrophages following VSV challenges in vitro.
source: The results in Figure 6B and C show that Tim-3 knockout significantly increased the expression of G3BP1 and TIA-1 at the protein level in macrophages following VSV challenges in vitro, demonstrating that Tim-3 inhibits the formation of SGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Tim-3 inhibits the formation of SGs.
source: The results in Figure 6B and C show that Tim-3 knockout significantly increased the expression of G3BP1 and TIA-1 at the protein level in macrophages following VSV challenges in vitro, demonstrating that Tim-3 inhibits the formation of SGs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing increased SG markers in Tim-3KO cells.

claim: The expression of SG markers, G3BP1 and TIA-1, and VSV replication are significantly changed in spleen, lung, and peritoneal macrophages from Tim-3KO mice compared to those in WT mice.
source: We found that the expression of SG markers, G3BP1 and TIA-1, and VSV replication were significantly changed in spleen, lung, and peritoneal macrophages from Tim-3KO mice than those in WT mice (Figure 7A–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A-I.

claim: Lethal VSV infections lead to an increased survival rate in Tim-3KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Also, lethal VSV infections led to an increased survival rate in Tim-3KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 7J) and a less severe tissue inflammation (Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Lethal VSV infections lead to less severe tissue inflammation in Tim-3KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Also, lethal VSV infections led to an increased survival rate in Tim-3KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 7J) and a less severe tissue inflammation (Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Tim-3 deficiency enhances the formation of SGs in vivo and protects mice from VSV.
source: These data showed that Tim-3 deficiency enhances the formation of SGs in vivo and protects mice from VSV.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the in vivo data showing increased SG markers and improved survival in Tim-3KO mice.

claim: Silencing of TRIM47 with specific siRNA in RAW264.7 leads to increased G3BP1 and TIA-1 expression and a decreased viral load following VSV infection.
source: The data showed that silencing of TRIM47 with specific siRNA in RAW264.7 led to increased G3BP1 and TIA-1 expression and a decreased viral load following VSV infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), further confirming that TRIM47 acts as an up-stream regulator of the NF90-SG antiviral pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRIM47 acts as an up-stream regulator of the NF90-SG antiviral pathway.
source: The data showed that silencing of TRIM47 with specific siRNA in RAW264.7 led to increased G3BP1 and TIA-1 expression and a decreased viral load following VSV infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), further confirming that TRIM47 acts as an up-stream regulator of the NF90-SG antiviral pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that TRIM47 knockdown increases SG markers and decreases viral load.

claim: Tim-3 is specifically upregulated following VSV infection.
source: In summary, we have verified that Tim-3 is specifically upregulated following VSV infection and inhibits NF90 signaling pathway in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1A and B showing increased Tim-3 expression after VSV infection.

claim: Tim-3 inhibits NF90 signaling pathway in macrophages.
source: In summary, we have verified that Tim-3 is specifically upregulated following VSV infection and inhibits NF90 signaling pathway in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing decreased NF90 expression and activity in the presence of Tim-3.

claim: Tim-3 promotes TRIM47-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of NF90 intracellularly.
source: Intracellularly, Tim-3 promotes TRIM47-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of NF90.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assays and degradation experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tim-3 signaling inhibits the formation and the activity of the NF90 downstream SGs in VSV-infected models.
source: In VSV-infected models, Tim-3 signaling inhibits the formation and the activity of the NF90 downstream SGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing decreased SG markers in the presence of Tim-3 and increased SG markers in Tim-3KO cells.

claim: This is the first report demonstrating the ubiquitination modification of NF90.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report demonstrating the ubiquitination modification of NF90.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: VSV is an RNA virus widely used for investigating anti-viral immunity in both mouse and human models.
source: To test whether Tim-3 is involved in the innate immunity against viruses, we challenged macrophages with VSV, an RNA virus widely used for investigating anti-viral immunity in both mouse and human models (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: NF90 is required for an efficient response against VSV infection.
source: One report showed that NF90 is required for an efficient response against VSV infection (Pfeifer et al., 2008), but the underlying mechanism has not been clarified.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pfeifer et al., 2008.

claim: NF90 interacts with the VP35 protein of Ebola virus (EBOV) and inhibits EBOV infection through impairing the function of the EBOV transcription/replication complex.
source: Other reports have shown that NF90 interacted with the VP35 protein of Ebola virus (EBOV) and inhibited EBOV infection through impairing the function of the EBOV transcription/replication complex (Shabman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shabman et al., 2011.

claim: Knockdown of NF90 in indicated cells dramatically promotes EBOV and influenza virus replication.
source: Knockdown of NF90 in indicated cells dramatically promotes EBOV and influenza virus replication, while overexpression of NF90 inhibits or impacts replication of these viruses (Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; and Wang et al., 2009.

claim: Overexpression of NF90 inhibits or impacts replication of EBOV and influenza viruses.
source: Knockdown of NF90 in indicated cells dramatically promotes EBOV and influenza virus replication, while overexpression of NF90 inhibits or impacts replication of these viruses (Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016; Shabman et al., 2011; and Wang et al., 2009.

claim: SGs, not the interferon pathway, serve as the downstream signaling cascade of the NF90 antiviral pathway.
source: When the signaling cascades were investigated, SGs, not the interferon pathway, served as the downstream signaling cascade of the NF90 antiviral pathway (Shabman et al., 2011; Pfeifer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shabman et al., 2011 and Pfeifer et al., 2008.

claim: NF90 promotes the assemblage of SG and synergizes with other proteins to exert antiviral immunity.
source: NF90 promotes (Meunier et al., 2014) the assemblage of SG and synergizes with other proteins to exert antiviral immunity (Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meunier et al., 2014 and Wen et al., 2014.

claim: Tim-3 induces apoptosis and T cell tolerance by binding with its ligand Gal-9.
source: Tim-3 is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that was initially found to be expressed on activated Th1 cells by binding with its ligand Gal-9 (Chou et al., 2009; Dardalhon et al., 2010). Tim-3 induces apoptosis and T cell tolerance (Nakayama et al., 2009; Sarraj et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chou et al., 2009; Dardalhon et al., 2010; Nakayama et al., 2009; and Sarraj et al., 2014.

claim: Dysregulated Tim-3 on innate immune cells contributes to the immune evasion of many tumors or pathogens.
source: Recently, our works and other published data have focused on the roles of Tim-3 in maintaining the homeostasis of innate immune cells and have demonstrated that the dysregulated Tim-3 on innate immune cells also contributes to the immune evasion of many tumors or pathogens (Diao et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Diao et al., 2020 and Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Tim-3 suppresses the macrophage-mediated antiviral immune response.
source: Here we have found that Tim-3 suppresses the macrophage-mediated antiviral immune response, suggesting that it is a potent therapeutic target for re-boosting innate immunity against viruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased viral loads in Tim-3 knockout macrophages.

claim: Tim-3 is a potent therapeutic target for re-boosting innate immunity against viruses.
source: Here we have found that Tim-3 suppresses the macrophage-mediated antiviral immune response, suggesting that it is a potent therapeutic target for re-boosting innate immunity against viruses.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: The intracellular tail of Tim-3 contains a highly conserved tyrosine-containing src homology 2 (SH2)-binding motif.
source: The intracellular tail of Tim-3 contains a highly conserved tyrosine-containing src homology 2 (SH2)-binding motif, and tyrosine residues within this motif can be phosphorylated, which is critical for Tim-3 signaling in T cells (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Tyrosine residues within the SH2-binding motif of Tim-3 can be phosphorylated, which is critical for Tim-3 signaling in T cells.
source: The intracellular tail of Tim-3 contains a highly conserved tyrosine-containing src homology 2 (SH2)-binding motif, and tyrosine residues within this motif can be phosphorylated, which is critical for Tim-3 signaling in T cells (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of Tim-3 tail or mutation of the conserved tyrosines, including Tyr265, Tyr272, Tyr280, and Try281, within Tim-3 tail significantly attenuates the interaction between Tim-3 and NF90.
source: We have also demonstrated that deletion of Tim-3 tail or mutation of the conserved tyrosines, including Tyr265, Tyr272, Tyr280, and Try281, within Tim-3 tail significantly attenuated the interaction between Tim-3 and NF90.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: NF90 possesses a DZF in the N-terminal region, which is a symbol of ubiquitination for substrates.
source: Structurally, NF90 possesses a DZF in the N-terminal region, which is a symbol of ubiquitination for substrates (Ji et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ji et al., 2018.

claim: Lys297 is a highly conserved residue among different isoforms of NF90.
source: Further, we have also found that Lys297, a highly conserved residue among different isoforms of NF90, plays a critical role in the K-48-linked ubiquitination of NF90.
evidence: This is a structural observation about NF90.

claim: Lys297 plays a critical role in the K-48-linked ubiquitination of NF90.
source: Further, we have also found that Lys297, a highly conserved residue among different isoforms of NF90, plays a critical role in the K-48-linked ubiquitination of NF90.
evidence: This claim is supported by site-directed mutagenesis data showing that K297R mutation blocks ubiquitination.

claim: TRIM47 contains a RING finger domain in the N-terminus, which may contribute to ubiquitin modification.
source: When the candidates accounting for NF90 ubiquitination were examined, we focused on TRIM47 as it got the highest scores and the highest number of matched peptides among NF90-interacting proteins, and structurally, TRIM47 contains a RING finger domain in the N-terminus, which may contribute to ubiquitin modification (Ji et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ji et al., 2018.

claim: TRIM family proteins play important roles in many biological processes, such as cell cycle regulation and viral response.
source: In addition, TRIM family proteins play important roles in many biological processes, such as cell cycle regulation and viral response (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Tim-3 may recruit TRIM47 using its SH2-binding domain as the tyrosines are phosphorylated following VSV infection.
source: We posit that Tim-3 may recruit TRIM47 using its SH2-binding domain as the tyrosines are phosphorylated following VSV infection.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural features of Tim-3 and the observed phosphorylation.

claim: Siglec-G triggers downstream signaling by recruiting SHP-2.
source: A recent report showing that Siglec-G triggers downstream signaling by recruiting SHP-2 (Chen et al., 2013) supports this hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: TRIM47 dose-dependently promotes the proteasome-dependent degradation of NF90.
source: Here we have demonstrated that TRIM47 dose-dependently promotes the proteasome-dependent degradation of NF90 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tim-3 enhances the expression and ubiquitination of TRIM47.
source: Interestingly, our data showed that Tim-3 enhances the expression and ubiquitination of TRIM47.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D, E, and F.

claim: This is the first report showing the ubiquitination modification of TRIM47.
source: This is also the first report showing the ubiquitination modification of TRIM47.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Tim-3 promotes tumor-prone macrophage polarization by binding to and suppressing the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of STAT1.
source: Huang et al., 2015 showed that Tim-3 induces T cell exhaustion via Human leucocyte antigen B associated transcript (BAT) and using CEACAM1 as a coreceptor, and our findings have shown that Tim-3 promotes tumor-prone macrophage polarization by binding to and suppressing the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of STAT1 (Jiang et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Tim-3 inhibits TLR4-mediated macrophage activation during sepsis by suppressing NF-kB activation.
source: Further, Tim-3 inhibits TLR4-mediated macrophage activation during sepsis by suppressing NF-kB activation (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2013.
